09-312.r: Commercial Paper (CP) → source of credit for corporate industry; introduced in India in 1990; unsecured promissory note; maturity 7 days to one year.

09-313.r: Convertible Bonds → pay a lower interest rate (option to swap for equity); the equity option gives some indexation to rising consumer prices. Both statements correct.

09-314.r: Indian Government bond yields are influenced by all three: US Federal Reserve actions, RBI actions (monetary policy), and inflation and short-term interest rates.

09-315.r: Inflation-Indexed Bonds (IIBs) → protect investors from inflation and let Government reduce coupon rates (cost saving); interest and capital gains on IIBs are not tax-free.

09-316.r: Blue Chip → shares of large, well-established, financially sound companies with dependable earnings, giving a consistently high rate of return.

09-317.r: Sweat Equity shares → issued to directors/employees at a discount or for non-cash consideration (know-how, IPR, value addition); a reward for their contribution.

09-318.r: Gilt-edged market → market of Government securities (G-secs); called 'gilt-edged' because interest payment and redemption on the due date are certain.
09-318.t: Don't confuse gilt-edged (Government securities) with bullion market (gold, silver).

09-320.r: SAPs (Structural Adjustment Programmes) → World Bank/IMF loan-linked policies for developing countries, not share market; Sensex, BSE, Nifty are share market terms.

09-321.r: NIKKEI (Nikkei 225) → share price index of the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Japan.

09-322.r: S&P 500 (Standard and Poor 500) → market-capitalization-weighted stock index of the 500 leading publicly traded companies of the United States.

09-323.r: Dow Jones → New York; FTSE-100 → London; Hang Seng → Hong Kong (not Seoul); KOSPI → Seoul.
09-323.t: Don't pair Hang Seng with Seoul: Hang Seng is Hong Kong, KOSPI is Seoul.

09-324.r: Wrong pair: Singapore–Shcomp. Shcomp = Shanghai index; Singapore's index = STI. Correct: Japan–Nikkei, U.K.–FTSE, U.S.A.–Nasdaq.

09-325.r: Brent Index → crude oil prices; Brent Complex = oil market around the North Sea of Northwest Europe.

09-326.r: Among USA, India, China, Japan → India's market-cap exceeded its GDP (2007; all-time high 146.4% of GDP in December 2007).

09-327.r: Dividend → declared on Subscribed Capital (the part of issued capital bought by shareholders); dividend = share of company's net profit paid to shareholders.
09-327.t: Not Issued or Authorized Capital; dividend goes on the capital actually subscribed by shareholders.

09-328.r: Debenture holders → creditors of the company; debenture = medium/long-term loan certificate carrying a fixed rate of interest.
09-328.t: Shareholders own the company; debenture holders only lend to it.

09-329.r: Debenture of a company → freely transferable, so ownership can change; LIC Policy, Bank Fixed Deposit, Kisan Vikas Patra → fixed ownership.

09-330.r: Balance sheet → snapshot of a company's financial condition at a point in time; shows size and composition of assets, liabilities and equity.

09-331.r: First Land Development Bank → Jhang (Punjab), 1920; gives long-term finance for land development and agricultural production.

09-332.r: Land Development Bank → long-term loans to farmers (land development, higher agricultural production).

09-335.r: Land Development Bank → part of the Cooperative Credit Structure (quasi-commercial), with State Cooperative Banks and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies.

09-336.r: Cooperative credit is three-tier: PACS (village level) → Central Cooperative Banks (district level) → State Cooperative Banks (state level).
09-336.h: V-D-S ladder: Village PACS, District CCB, State StCB.

09-339.r: Urban Cooperative Banks → can issue equity and preference shares; under Banking Regulation Act, 1949 via 1966 amendment; regulated by RCS/CRCS and RBI, not local boards.

09-340.c: Book gives no single answer: there were 1618 UCBs at end-March 2012; option (c) 1645 is the end-March 2011 figure.

09-341.r: Consumer Cooperative Stores → set up by the members; registered by the Registrar of Cooperative Societies.

09-342.r: All four (NABARD, RRB, SBI, Allahabad Bank) give direct finance; NABARD lends directly to food parks, warehouses, cold chains, not to individuals.

09-343.r: NABARD → set up July 1982, during the Sixth Five Year Plan; HQ Mumbai; apex bank for agricultural refinance.
hi: NABARD (राष्ट्रीय कृषि और ग्रामीण विकास बैंक)

09-349.r: NABARD → apex body for all credit needs of agriculture and rural development; set up 12 July 1982 under Act 61 of 1981; gives refinance.

09-358.r: NABARD refinances Scheduled Commercial Banks, RRBs and State Land Development Banks; it does not refinance the Export-Import Bank.

09-359.r: NABARD → nodal agency for the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF); RIDF created 1995-96 with initial corpus of Rs. 2000 crore.

09-360.r: First RRB → Prathama Grameen Bank, Moradabad (U.P.), 2 October 1975; the other first four: Malda, Gorakhpur, Bhiwani, Jaipur.
09-360.h: RRBs born on Gandhi Jayanti (2 October) 1975.

09-362.r: Taking over the Agricultural Refinance Corporation of India's functions → not an RRB function; RRBs lend to small/marginal farmers and rural people, supplementing commercial banks.

09-363.r: Direct credit to rural households → Regional Rural Banks and Land Development Banks; NABARD gives no direct credit, it refinances other institutions.
09-363.t: Don't confuse NABARD's refinance role with direct lending to households.

09-364.r: Chronology: RRB (1975) → NABARD (1982) → SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (1992-93) → Kisan Credit Card (1998).

09-365.r: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme → started by NABARD in 1992-93; implemented by Commercial Banks, RRBs and Cooperative Banks, not by NABARD.

09-366.r: SHG programme → originally initiated by NABARD (not SBI); SHG members jointly take responsibility for a member's loan; RRBs and Scheduled Commercial Banks support SHGs.

09-367.r: Bhandari Committee (1994) → restructuring of Regional Rural Banks; identified 49 RRBs for restructuring; more powers to RRB Boards.

09-368.r: Narasimham Committees (1991, Financial System; 1997, Banking Sector Reforms) → financial sector reforms; suggested reducing SLR and CRR.

09-371.r: Committee on Financial Sector Reforms → headed by Raghuram Rajan; set up 2007 by the Planning Commission; report submitted 2008.

09-372.r: Raghuram Rajan Committee (2007) → Financial Sector Reforms.

09-373.r: Bimal Jalan Panel → RBI's three-member committee to scrutinize applications for new bank licenses; report 25 February 2014.

09-374.r: First Chairman, Disinvestment Commission (1996) → G.V. Ramkrishna; it gave 13 reports covering privatization of 57 public sector units.

09-375.r: Rangarajan Committee (1993) → disinvestment of Government shares in public sector companies.

09-377.r: Abhijit Sen working group (2007) → revision of the Wholesale Price Index series; report May 2008; recommended base year 2004-05.

09-378.r: Financial Stability and Development Council (December 2010) → headed by Union Finance Minister; monitors macroprudential supervision; not an organ of NITI Aayog.

09-379.r: Swabhimaan Campaign (10 February 2011) → financial inclusion; take banking to the doorsteps of the rural poor.

09-381.r: Business Correspondent (Bank Saathi) → villagers in branchless areas can draw subsidies/social security benefits and make deposits and withdrawals; both correct.

09-382.r: Gold Monetization Scheme and Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme (2015) → bring idle household gold into the economy; cut dependence on gold imports; not to promote FDI.

09-383.r: Kisan Credit Card (August 1998) → covers both consumption and investment credit of farmers; run by Commercial Banks, RRBs, Small Finance Banks, Cooperatives.

09-385.r: Banking Ombudsman → appointed by RBI; free of fee; NRIs with Indian accounts can complain; its orders are NOT final and binding on the parties.

09-387.r: CRISIL, CARE and ICRA → all are credit rating agencies in India.

09-388.r: Credit rating agencies, oldest first: CRISIL (1987) → ICRA (1991) → CARE (1993).

09-389.r: CRISIL (Credit Rating Information Services of India Ltd., 1987) → evaluates the creditworthiness of companies; one of India's oldest credit rating agencies.

09-390.r: Phillips Curve (A.W. Phillips, 1958) → stable inverse relation between inflation and unemployment; a short-run trade-off.

09-391.r: 'Smart Money' → term used for credit card.

09-392.r: 'Plastic Money' → credit cards (mainly bank-issued), also debit, prepaid, smart and store cards used in place of bank notes.

09-394.r: PIN → Personal Identification Number; numeric code issued with a payment card that adds a layer of security to electronic transactions.

09-395.r: Credit card of a nationalized bank → NOT a prepaid payment instrument; Delhi Metro Rail Card, e-wallet, Airtel Money → prepaid instruments.
09-395.t: Credit card = pay later on credit; prepaid instrument = pay first, then use.

09-396.r: Prices → indispensable for the existence of a market (goods and services are bought and sold on the basis of price).

09-397.r: Market as an economic tendency → leads to consumerism.

09-398.r: Buyer's market → supply exceeds demand; buyers have the advantage over sellers in price bargaining.

09-399.r: Accounting → 'language of business' (communicates financial information); it gives all information a businessman needs. A and R true, R explains A.

09-400.r: Condition → stipulation essential to the contract's main purpose; breach allows repudiation. Warranty → collateral; breach gives damages only. So A true, R false.
09-400.t: Don't swap them: breach of condition → repudiate contract; breach of warranty → claim damages.

09-401.r: Merchandise Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold/Average Stock; Current Ratio = Current Assets/Current Liabilities; Acid Test = Liquid Assets/Current Liabilities; Return on Total Assets = NPBIT/Total Assets.
09-401.c: Book gives no single answer because item D should read 'Return on Total Assets/Capital Employed', not 'Gross Capital Employed'; otherwise its matching gives (b) 4 1 2 3.

09-402.r: Auctions and dynamic (real-time) pricing markets → the book accepts both B2B and C2C commerce.

09-403.r: C2B (consumer-to-business) model → consumers fix their own price and the business accepts or declines; opposite of the traditional B2C model.

09-404.r: Vegetables, flowers, fruits → very short period market (supply fixed; price depends on demand).

09-405.r: Supply-side economics → producer's point of view; production (supply) drives growth; tax cuts for the wealthy trickle down to the economy.

09-406.r: Total product constant → marginal product is zero (total product at its optimum level).
09-406.h: MP = extra output from one more unit; no change in TP means MP is zero.

09-407.r: Consumer equilibrium → consumer fulfils his needs with a given level of income and cannot gain by changing what he buys.

09-408.r: Demand for a good rises if its substitute's price rises or its own price falls; not if a complement's price rises or income rises for an inferior good.

09-409.r: Fixed demand + rising supply → price likely to decrease (supply and price inversely related).

09-410.r: General price level rises with all three: higher money supply, lower aggregate output, higher effective demand.

09-411.r: Money supply fixed + demand for money rises → rate of interest rises.

09-412.r: Price-hike → businessmen make profit (A true); consumers curtail needs as money's purchasing power falls (R true); R does not explain A.

09-413.r: Profit Volume (P/V) ratio = contribution as % of sales; improved by raising selling price, altering sales mix and reducing variable cost (all).

09-414.r: 'Shadow Prices' for pricing public goods → J. Tinbergen; shadow price = estimated true (equilibrium) value of something not normally priced in the market.

09-415.r: Cars → not a public good; Government administration, national defence and roads → public goods.

09-416.r: Commodity given free by Government (street light, free education) → opportunity cost shifts from its consumers to the tax-paying public.

09-417.r: Trade → exchange of goods/services for money; represents both demand and supply, not only demand.

09-418.r: Commerce → removes impediments to exchange and deals with delivering products to consumers (distribution, not production); both statements correct.

10-001.r: Theory of three stages of social development → Auguste Comte: theological → metaphysical → positive (scientific) stage.
10-001.h: Comte's T-M-P: Theology, Metaphysics, Positive science.

10-002.r: HDI and SDG rankings of Indian States → positively related, since SDG targets are closely tied to education and health. A and R true, R explains A.

10-003.r: Development measures in order: Per-capita Income (US, 1934, Simon Kuznets' team) → PQLI (Physical Quality of Life Index) → HDI (Human Development Index).

10-004.r: PQLI → Morris D. Morris (mid-1970s); average of basic literacy, infant mortality and life expectancy; best pair for physical quality of life: infant mortality–literacy.

10-006.r: Human Development Report → published by UNDP; first HDR released in 1990.

10-007.r: HDI → developed by Pakistani economist Mahbub-ul-Haq for UNDP's Human Development Report (first 1990); rooted in Amartya Sen's capability work.

10-009.r: Capability Approach → Prof. Amartya Sen (1980s); alternative to welfare economics, focusing on people's capability to live lives they value.

10-010.r: UNDP → first to focus on the human aspect of development; first Human Development Report in 1990.

10-011.r: HDI = composite of life expectancy, education and per capita income (per capita GNI since 2010; per capita GDP before); published by UNDP; value from zero to 1.

10-012.r: Old HDI → literacy rate, life expectancy at birth, GDP per head at real purchasing power; since 2010 → life expectancy, mean and expected years of schooling, income.
10-012.c: Book gives no single answer: (b) GDP per head at real purchasing power was right when asked; since 2010 the HDI uses GNI per capita (PPP $).

10-013.r: HDI life expectancy goalposts → 85 and 25 years before 2010; now 85 and 20 years (index = 1 at 85, 0 at 20).
10-013.c: Book gives no single answer: (c) 85 and 25 years were the goalposts before 2010, when this was asked; they are now 85 and 20 years.

10-014.r: HDI indicators → life expectancy at birth, education level, standard of living (GNI per capita PPP $); not included → social inequality, health and nutrition, urbanization.
10-014.c: Book gives no single answer: social inequality (c) is not an HDI indicator, and adult literacy (d) was dropped in 2010, so both now fit.

10-019.r: HDI ranks for 2021 (HDR 2021/2022): Hong Kong 4th, Australia 5th, Japan 19th, Russia 52nd → descending order: Hong Kong, Australia, Japan, Russia.

10-020.r: HDR 2021/2022 → India's HDI rank slipped from 130 (2020) to 132 in 2021, not 2022 (191 countries); HDR 2023/2024 → 134 in 2022.
10-020.t: Both statements wrong: 'upgraded' is wrong and the year 2022 is wrong.

10-021.r: HDI 2019 ranks (HDR 2020): Brazil 84, China 85, South Africa 114, India 131 → ascending: Brazil, China, South Africa, India.

10-023.r: HDR 2015 → India 130th; HDI uses life expectancy, education and per capita income; India lowest among BRICS. Book marks all three correct.
10-023.c: HDR 2015 ranked India 130th of 188 countries, not 183, so statement A is strictly wrong and (b) would fit; the book still marks (d).

10-024.r: HDR 2018 → Norway ranked first in HDI (for 2017); HDR 2023/2024 → Switzerland 1st (0.967), Norway 2nd, for 2022.

10-025.r: HDR 2015 → India 130th of 188 (HDI for 2014), UPPSC's answer; HDR 2014 → 135th of 187 (for 2013); HDR 2023/2024 → 134th of 193.
10-025.c: Book gives no single answer: UPPSC accepted 130th (HDR 2015, of 188); HDR 2014 gave 135th of 187. Neither report had 186 countries.
